notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Physiology is the branch of biology that studies the functions of living organisms and their parts.
  • Anatomy deals mainly with structure, while physiology deals mainly with function.
  • Human physiology explains how cells, tissues, organs and organ systems work together.
  • Normal body functions depend on coordination among the nervous, endocrine, circulatory, respiratory, digestive and excretory systems.
  • Maintenance of a stable internal environment is called homeostasis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anatomy → Structure

Physiology → Function

2. Homeostasis
  • Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within suitable limits.
  • Body temperature is regulated homeostatically.
  • Blood glucose is regulated homeostatically.
  • Blood pH is regulated within a narrow range.
  • Water and electrolyte concentrations are also controlled.
  • Negative-feedback mechanisms are central to homeostasis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Homeostasis → Stable Internal Environment

3. Claude Bernard
  • Claude Bernard developed the concept of a stable internal environment.
  • He used the term milieu intérieur for the internal environment.
  • His work laid foundations for modern physiology.
4. Walter Cannon
  • Walter Bradford Cannon popularised the term homeostasis.
  • He also studied the body's fight-or-flight response.
  • Cannon's work linked nervous and hormonal regulation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Walter Cannon → Homeostasis

5. Major Human Organ Systems

Important systems are:

  • Digestive system.
  • Respiratory system.
  • Circulatory system.
  • Excretory/urinary system.
  • Nervous system.
  • Endocrine system.
  • Musculoskeletal system.
  • Reproductive system.
  • Integumentary system.
  • Immune and lymphatic systems.
6. Blood
  • Blood is a fluid connective tissue.
  • It transports oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones and wastes.
  • It helps regulate body temperature and pH.
  • It participates in immunity and blood clotting.
  • An adult human has roughly 5 litres of blood, though the amount varies with body size.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blood → Fluid Connective Tissue

7. Components of Blood

Blood consists of:

  • Plasma.
  • Red blood cells.
  • White blood cells.
  • Platelets.
  • Plasma makes up approximately 55% of blood volume.
  • Formed elements make up approximately 45%.
8. Plasma
  • Plasma is the liquid component of blood.
  • It is approximately 90% water.
  • It contains proteins, salts, nutrients, hormones, gases and waste products.
  • Major plasma proteins include albumin, globulins and fibrinogen.
9. Albumin
  • Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein.
  • It helps maintain colloid osmotic pressure.
  • It also transports several substances in blood.
10. Globulins
  • Some globulins participate in transport.
  • Immunoglobulins are antibodies.
  • They play an important role in immune defence.
11. Fibrinogen
  • Fibrinogen is a soluble plasma protein.
  • It is converted into fibrin during blood clotting.
  • Fibrin forms a mesh that helps stabilise a blood clot.
12. Serum
  • Serum is plasma after clotting factors such as fibrinogen have been largely removed.
  • Plasma contains fibrinogen.
  • Serum does not contain significant fibrinogen.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Plasma ≠ Serum.

13. Red Blood Cells
  • Red blood cells are also called erythrocytes.
  • Mature human RBCs are biconcave discs.
  • Mature mammalian RBCs normally lack nuclei.
  • They contain haemoglobin.
  • Their main function is oxygen transport.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

RBC → Erythrocyte → Haemoglobin → Oxygen

14. Haemoglobin
  • Haemoglobin is an iron-containing respiratory pigment.
  • It is located inside red blood cells.
  • Oxygen combines reversibly with haemoglobin.
  • Oxygenated haemoglobin is called oxyhaemoglobin.
  • Iron in haemoglobin is essential for oxygen binding.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Haemoglobin → Iron

15. RBC Formation
  • Red blood-cell formation is called erythropoiesis.
  • In adults, it occurs mainly in red bone marrow.
  • The kidneys release erythropoietin when oxygen availability is low.
  • Erythropoietin stimulates increased RBC production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Erythropoietin → Kidney → RBC Production

16. RBC Lifespan
  • Average human red blood-cell lifespan is about 120 days.
  • Old RBCs are removed mainly by the spleen and liver.
  • Iron from haemoglobin can be recycled.
📌 Must-Memorise

RBC Lifespan → ~120 Days

17. Spleen
  • The spleen filters blood.
  • It removes aged or damaged red blood cells.
  • It participates in immune responses.
  • It stores some platelets and blood cells.
  • It is sometimes called the graveyard of RBCs in traditional textbooks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spleen → Removal of Old RBCs

18. White Blood Cells
  • White blood cells are also called leukocytes.
  • They are involved in defence against infection and foreign substances.
  • Unlike mature RBCs, they possess nuclei.
  • They can migrate out of blood vessels into tissues.
19. Major White Blood Cell Types

Granulocytes:

  • Neutrophils.
  • Eosinophils.
  • Basophils.

Agranulocytes:

  • Lymphocytes.
  • Monocytes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Granulocytes → N E B

Agranulocytes → L M

20. Neutrophils
  • Neutrophils are the most abundant circulating white blood cells in healthy adults.
  • They engulf and destroy bacteria and cellular debris.
  • They are important in acute inflammatory responses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Most Abundant WBC → Neutrophil

21. Lymphocytes

Important lymphocytes include:

  • B cells.
  • T cells.
  • Natural killer cells.
  • B cells can produce antibodies through plasma cells.
  • T cells coordinate and execute cell-mediated immunity.
22. Monocytes
  • Monocytes are large circulating WBCs.
  • They can enter tissues and differentiate into macrophages.
  • Macrophages engulf pathogens and cellular debris.
23. Eosinophils
  • Eosinophils are particularly involved in defence against certain parasites.
  • They also participate in allergic reactions.
24. Basophils
  • Basophils release inflammatory mediators such as histamine.
  • They participate in allergic and inflammatory responses.
25. Platelets
  • Platelets are also called thrombocytes.
  • They are cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes in bone marrow.
  • They play a major role in blood clotting.
  • They form an initial platelet plug at injured blood vessels.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Platelets → Blood Clotting

26. Blood Clotting
  • Blood clotting is also called coagulation.
  • Platelets become activated at sites of injury.
  • A series of clotting reactions converts prothrombin to thrombin.
  • Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin.
  • Fibrin stabilises the clot.
📌 Memory

Prothrombin → Thrombin

Fibrinogen → Fibrin

27. Vitamin K and Clotting
  • Vitamin K is required for synthesis of several clotting factors.
  • Deficiency can impair normal blood clotting.
  • The liver synthesises many clotting proteins.
28. Blood pH
  • Normal arterial blood pH is approximately 7.35–7.45.
  • Blood is therefore slightly alkaline.
  • Buffers, lungs and kidneys cooperate to regulate pH.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blood pH → ~7.4

29. Heart
  • The human heart is a muscular pumping organ.
  • It lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs.
  • Most of it lies slightly to the left of the body's midline.
  • It is approximately the size of a person's fist.
  • The heart is enclosed by the pericardium.
30. Pericardium
  • Pericardium is the membrane surrounding the heart.
  • Pericardial fluid reduces friction during heart movements.
31. Heart Chambers

The human heart has four chambers:

  • Right atrium.
  • Right ventricle.
  • Left atrium.
  • Left ventricle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Human Heart → 4 Chambers

32. Atria
  • Atria are the upper chambers.
  • Right atrium receives deoxygenated systemic blood.
  • Left atrium receives oxygenated blood from lungs.
33. Ventricles
  • Ventricles are the lower pumping chambers.
  • Right ventricle pumps blood to lungs.
  • Left ventricle pumps blood to the systemic circulation.
  • Left ventricular wall is thicker than right ventricular wall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Thickest Heart Wall → Left Ventricle

34. Heart Valves

Major valves are:

  • Tricuspid valve.
  • Mitral/bicuspid valve.
  • Pulmonary semilunar valve.
  • Aortic semilunar valve.
  • Valves prevent backward flow of blood.
35. Tricuspid Valve
  • Tricuspid valve lies between right atrium and right ventricle.
  • It prevents backflow into the right atrium during ventricular contraction.
36. Mitral Valve
  • Mitral or bicuspid valve lies between left atrium and left ventricle.
  • It contains two major cusps.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Right AV Valve → Tricuspid

Left AV Valve → Bicuspid/Mitral

37. Pulmonary Artery
  • Pulmonary artery carries blood from right ventricle to lungs.
  • It carries deoxygenated blood in normal adult circulation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Pulmonary artery → Deoxygenated blood.

38. Pulmonary Veins
  • Pulmonary veins carry blood from lungs to left atrium.
  • They carry oxygenated blood.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Pulmonary veins → Oxygenated blood.

39. Aorta
  • Aorta is the largest artery in the human body.
  • It carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Largest Artery → Aorta

40. Venae Cavae
  • Superior vena cava returns blood from upper body.
  • Inferior vena cava returns blood from lower body.
  • Both enter the right atrium.
41. Coronary Circulation
  • Coronary arteries supply oxygen and nutrients to heart muscle.
  • Coronary veins drain blood from heart tissue.
  • The myocardium requires continuous blood supply.
42. Double Circulation

Humans possess double circulation:

  • Pulmonary circulation.
  • Systemic circulation.
  • Blood passes through the heart twice during one complete circuit.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Human Circulation → Double Circulation

43. Pulmonary Circulation

Path:

Right ventricle → Pulmonary artery → Lungs → Pulmonary veins → Left atrium

  • Its main purpose is gas exchange.
44. Systemic Circulation

Path:

Left ventricle → Aorta → Body tissues → Venae cavae → Right atrium

  • It supplies body tissues with oxygen and nutrients.
45. Hepatic Portal Circulation
  • Hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from digestive organs to liver.
  • The liver processes absorbed nutrients before blood enters general circulation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hepatic Portal Vein → Intestine to Liver

46. Heartbeat
  • One heartbeat consists of contraction and relaxation.
  • Contraction is called systole.
  • Relaxation is called diastole.
  • A normal resting adult heart rate is often around 60–100 beats per minute.
  • The traditional textbook average is approximately 72 beats per minute.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Systole → Contraction

Diastole → Relaxation

47. Cardiac Cycle
  • Cardiac cycle includes atrial systole, ventricular systole and relaxation.
  • At about 75 beats per minute, one cardiac cycle lasts roughly 0.8 second.
48. Pacemaker of Heart
  • Sinoatrial node is the normal pacemaker of the heart.
  • It is located in the right atrium.
  • It generates electrical impulses that initiate each heartbeat.
📌 Must-Memorise

Natural Pacemaker → SA Node

49. AV Node
  • Atrioventricular node delays electrical conduction briefly.
  • This allows atria to empty before ventricles contract.
  • The impulse then travels through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.
50. ECG
  • ECG stands for electrocardiogram/electrocardiography depending on context.
  • It records electrical activity of the heart.
  • P wave represents atrial depolarisation.
  • QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation.
  • T wave represents ventricular repolarisation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ECG → Electrical Activity of Heart

51. Heart Sounds
  • First heart sound is associated mainly with closure of atrioventricular valves.
  • It is commonly described as “lub.”
  • Second heart sound is associated mainly with closure of semilunar valves.
  • It is commonly described as “dub.”
📌 Memory

Lub → AV Valves Close

Dub → Semilunar Valves Close

52. Blood Pressure
  • Blood pressure is the pressure exerted by blood on arterial walls.
  • Systolic pressure is the maximum arterial pressure during ventricular contraction.
  • Diastolic pressure is the lower pressure during ventricular relaxation.
  • A commonly cited normal adult value is approximately 120/80 mmHg.
📌 Must-Memorise

Normal Reference BP → ~120/80 mmHg

53. Sphygmomanometer
  • Blood pressure is measured using a sphygmomanometer.
  • Pressure is traditionally expressed in millimetres of mercury, mmHg.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blood Pressure Instrument → Sphygmomanometer

54. Arteries
  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
  • Their walls are generally thick, elastic and muscular.
  • Most arteries carry oxygenated blood.
  • Pulmonary arteries are the major exception in adult circulation.
55. Veins
  • Veins carry blood toward the heart.
  • Their walls are thinner than arteries.
  • Many veins have valves that prevent backflow.
  • Most veins carry deoxygenated blood.
  • Pulmonary veins are major exceptions.
56. Capillaries
  • Capillaries are microscopic blood vessels.
  • Their walls are extremely thin.
  • Exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes occurs across capillary walls.
  • Capillary walls are essentially one endothelial cell layer thick.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Capillaries → Exchange Vessels

57. Lymph
  • Lymph is a clear fluid derived from tissue fluid.
  • It returns excess tissue fluid to the bloodstream.
  • It transports absorbed fats from the intestine.
  • It carries immune cells.
58. Lacteals
  • Lacteals are lymphatic vessels present within intestinal villi.
  • They absorb much of the dietary fat from the small intestine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lacteals → Fat Absorption

59. Respiratory System

The respiratory system includes:

  • Nose/nasal cavity.
  • Pharynx.
  • Larynx.
  • Trachea.
  • Bronchi.
  • Bronchioles.
  • Lungs.
  • Alveoli.
60. Nose
  • Nasal hairs and mucus help trap particles.
  • Nasal passages warm and humidify inhaled air.
  • Olfactory receptors detect smell.
61. Pharynx
  • Pharynx is a common passage involved in both respiratory and digestive pathways.
  • Air moves from nasal cavity through pharynx toward larynx.
62. Larynx
  • Larynx is commonly called the voice box.
  • It contains vocal folds.
  • It connects pharynx with trachea.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Larynx → Voice Box

63. Epiglottis
  • Epiglottis is a flap associated with the entrance to the larynx.
  • During swallowing, it helps prevent food from entering the airway.
64. Trachea
  • Trachea is commonly called the windpipe.
  • C-shaped cartilage rings help keep it open.
  • Its lining contains mucus and cilia that help remove particles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Trachea → Windpipe

65. Bronchi
  • Trachea divides into right and left primary bronchi.
  • Bronchi enter the lungs.
  • They branch repeatedly into smaller bronchi and bronchioles.
66. Alveoli
  • Alveoli are microscopic air sacs.
  • They are the principal sites of gas exchange.
  • Their walls are thin.
  • They are surrounded by dense capillary networks.
  • Large surface area facilitates gas exchange.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alveoli → Gas Exchange

67. Surfactant
  • Pulmonary surfactant reduces surface tension inside alveoli.
  • It helps prevent alveolar collapse.
  • It is produced mainly by type II alveolar cells.
68. Lungs
  • Humans have two lungs.
  • Right lung usually has three lobes.
  • Left lung usually has two lobes.
  • The left lung has a cardiac notch accommodating the heart.
📌 Must-Memorise

Right Lung → 3 Lobes

Left Lung → 2 Lobes

69. Pleura
  • Each lung is enclosed by a double-layered pleural membrane.
  • Pleural fluid reduces friction during breathing.
70. Diaphragm
  • Diaphragm is a dome-shaped skeletal muscle below the lungs.
  • It is the principal muscle of quiet inspiration.
  • When it contracts, it flattens and increases thoracic volume.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Main Breathing Muscle → Diaphragm

71. Inspiration
  • During quiet inspiration, diaphragm contracts.
  • External intercostal muscles assist.
  • Thoracic volume increases.
  • Intrapulmonary pressure falls.
  • Air enters the lungs.
72. Expiration
  • Quiet expiration is usually passive.
  • Diaphragm relaxes.
  • Thoracic volume decreases.
  • Elastic recoil of lungs helps expel air.
73. Gas Exchange
  • Oxygen and carbon dioxide move mainly by diffusion.
  • Oxygen moves from alveoli into pulmonary capillary blood.
  • Carbon dioxide moves from blood into alveoli.
74. Oxygen Transport
  • Most oxygen in blood is carried bound to haemoglobin.
  • A small amount is dissolved directly in plasma.
  • Oxyhaemoglobin forms in lungs.
75. Carbon Dioxide Transport

Carbon dioxide is transported mainly:

  • As bicarbonate ions.
  • Bound to haemoglobin/proteins.
  • Dissolved in plasma.
  • Most CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Major CO₂ Transport Form → Bicarbonate

76. Respiratory Pigment
  • Human respiratory pigment is haemoglobin.
  • It contains iron.
  • It gives blood its red colour.
77. Respiratory Control Centre
  • Basic breathing rhythm is controlled by centres in the medulla oblongata and pons.
  • Carbon dioxide and hydrogen-ion levels strongly influence ventilation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Breathing Control → Medulla + Pons

78. Tidal Volume
  • Tidal volume is the volume of air inhaled or exhaled during a normal quiet breath.
  • A typical adult value is approximately 500 mL.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tidal Volume → ~500 mL

79. Vital Capacity
  • Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inspiration.
  • It varies with age, sex, body size and fitness.
  • A typical adult value is several litres.
80. Spirometer
  • A spirometer measures respiratory volumes and capacities.
  • It is used to evaluate lung function.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lung Volume Instrument → Spirometer

81. Digestive System

The alimentary canal includes:

  • Mouth.
  • Pharynx.
  • Oesophagus.
  • Stomach.
  • Small intestine.
  • Large intestine.
  • Rectum.
  • Anus.

Accessory organs include:

  • Salivary glands.
  • Liver.
  • Gallbladder.
  • Pancreas.
82. Digestion
  • Digestion breaks complex food molecules into simpler absorbable molecules.
  • Mechanical digestion physically breaks food.
  • Chemical digestion uses enzymes and other secretions.
  • Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.
83. Mouth
  • Digestion begins in the mouth.
  • Teeth mechanically break food.
  • Saliva moistens food.
  • The tongue helps mix food and form a bolus.
84. Saliva
  • Saliva is produced by salivary glands.
  • It contains water, mucus and enzymes.
  • Salivary amylase begins starch digestion.
  • Saliva also assists lubrication and oral hygiene.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Salivary Amylase → Starch Digestion

85. Salivary Glands

Major paired glands are:

  • Parotid.
  • Submandibular.
  • Sublingual.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Largest Salivary Gland → Parotid

86. Oesophagus
  • Oesophagus carries food from pharynx to stomach.
  • Food movement occurs through peristalsis.
  • No major digestion occurs in the oesophagus.
87. Peristalsis
  • Peristalsis is wave-like contraction of smooth muscle.
  • It moves food through the alimentary canal.
  • It is involuntary.
88. Stomach
  • Stomach stores and mixes food.
  • Gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, enzymes and mucus.
  • Protein digestion begins significantly in the stomach.
  • The acidic environment helps activate pepsin.
89. Hydrochloric Acid in Stomach
  • Hydrochloric acid creates a strongly acidic environment.
  • It helps convert pepsinogen to pepsin.
  • It helps destroy many ingested microorganisms.
  • It does not itself digest protein enzymatically.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gastric Acid → HCl

90. Pepsin
  • Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme.
  • It is secreted initially as inactive pepsinogen.
  • Acidic conditions activate pepsinogen.
  • Pepsin breaks proteins into smaller peptides.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pepsin → Protein Digestion → Stomach

91. Gastric Mucus
  • Mucus protects stomach lining from acid and digestive enzymes.
  • Bicarbonate near the mucosal surface also contributes to protection.
92. Small Intestine

Three parts are:

  • Duodenum.
  • Jejunum.
  • Ileum.
  • Most digestion and nutrient absorption occurs here.
📌 Must-Memorise

Small Intestine → Duodenum + Jejunum + Ileum

93. Duodenum
  • Duodenum receives chyme from stomach.
  • It receives bile.
  • It receives pancreatic juice.
  • Acidic chyme is neutralised by bicarbonate-rich secretions.
94. Pancreas
  • Pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine functions.
  • Exocrine pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate.
  • Endocrine pancreas secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pancreas → Mixed Gland

95. Pancreatic Enzymes

Major enzymes include:

  • Pancreatic amylase → Carbohydrates.
  • Trypsin/chymotrypsin → Proteins.
  • Pancreatic lipase → Fats.
  • Nucleases → Nucleic acids.
96. Liver
  • Liver is the largest internal gland in the human body.
  • It produces bile.
  • It stores glycogen.
  • It helps detoxify many substances.
  • It converts ammonia to urea.
  • It processes nutrients absorbed from the intestine.
📌 Must-Memorise

Largest Gland → Liver

97. Bile
  • Bile is produced by the liver.
  • It is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder.
  • Bile salts emulsify fats.
  • Bile does not contain digestive enzymes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bile → No digestive enzyme.

98. Gallbladder
  • Gallbladder stores and concentrates bile.
  • It releases bile into the small intestine.
  • The liver produces bile even if the gallbladder is absent.
99. Fat Emulsification
  • Bile salts break large fat droplets into smaller droplets.
  • This increases surface area for lipase.
  • Emulsification is physical, not enzymatic digestion.
100. Intestinal Villi
  • Villi are finger-like projections lining the small intestine.
  • They greatly increase absorptive surface area.
  • Blood capillaries absorb sugars and amino acids.
  • Lacteals absorb many dietary lipids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Villi → Nutrient Absorption

101. Large Intestine
  • Large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes.
  • It houses a large microbial population.
  • Faeces are formed and stored before elimination.
  • Major parts include caecum, colon and rectum.
102. Appendix
  • Vermiform appendix is attached to the caecum.
  • It contains lymphoid tissue.
  • It is not simply a completely useless organ.
103. Excretory System

Major urinary organs are:

  • Two kidneys.
  • Two ureters.
  • Urinary bladder.
  • Urethra.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Urinary System → Kidney → Ureter → Bladder → Urethra

104. Kidney
  • Kidneys are bean-shaped organs.
  • They are located toward the back of the abdominal cavity.
  • They filter blood.
  • They regulate water, electrolytes and acid-base balance.
  • They excrete nitrogenous wastes.
105. Functional Unit of Kidney
  • Nephron is the structural and functional unit of kidney.
  • Each human kidney contains roughly one million nephrons.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kidney Functional Unit → Nephron

106. Nephron Parts

Important parts include:

  • Bowman's capsule.
  • Glomerulus.
  • Proximal convoluted tubule.
  • Loop of Henle.
  • Distal convoluted tubule.
  • Collecting duct.
107. Glomerulus
  • Glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries.
  • Blood filtration begins here.
  • Filtrate passes into Bowman's capsule.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Glomerulus → Ultrafiltration

108. Bowman's Capsule
  • Bowman's capsule surrounds the glomerulus.
  • It receives glomerular filtrate.
  • Together, glomerulus and Bowman's capsule form the renal corpuscle.
109. Urine Formation

Three major processes are:

  • Glomerular filtration.
  • Tubular reabsorption.
  • Tubular secretion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Urine Formation → Filtration + Reabsorption + Secretion

110. Tubular Reabsorption
  • Useful substances are returned from nephron filtrate to blood.
  • Most glucose and amino acids are normally reabsorbed.
  • Large amounts of water and salts are also reabsorbed.
111. Tubular Secretion
  • Certain substances are actively secreted from blood into nephron tubules.
  • It helps regulate potassium, hydrogen ions and other substances.
  • It contributes to acid-base regulation.
112. Loop of Henle
  • Loop of Henle helps create an osmotic gradient in the kidney medulla.
  • This allows production of concentrated urine.
  • It operates through countercurrent mechanisms.
113. ADH
  • ADH stands for antidiuretic hormone.
  • It is also called vasopressin.
  • It is synthesised in the hypothalamus.
  • It is released from the posterior pituitary.
  • It increases water reabsorption in collecting ducts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ADH → Water Reabsorption ↑ → Urine Volume ↓

114. Aldosterone
  • Aldosterone is secreted by adrenal cortex.
  • It increases sodium reabsorption in distal nephron regions.
  • Water tends to follow retained sodium.
  • It also promotes potassium excretion.
115. Urea
  • Urea is the major nitrogenous waste in humans.
  • It is formed mainly in the liver.
  • It is produced from toxic ammonia through the urea cycle.
  • Kidneys excrete urea in urine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Urea Formation → Liver

Urea Excretion → Kidney

116. Normal Urine
  • Urine is mainly water.
  • It contains urea, salts, creatinine and other wastes.
  • Normal urine generally contains little or no glucose.
  • Average daily urine volume is often around 1–2 litres depending on fluid balance.
117. Ureter
  • Ureters transport urine from kidneys to urinary bladder.
  • Peristaltic contractions help move urine.
118. Urinary Bladder
  • Urinary bladder temporarily stores urine.
  • Its wall contains smooth muscle.
  • Urination is called micturition.
119. Dialysis
  • Dialysis removes wastes and excess fluid when kidneys cannot adequately perform these functions.
  • Haemodialysis filters blood through an artificial membrane.
  • Dialysis substitutes for some kidney functions but does not perfectly reproduce all kidney activities.
120. Artificial Kidney
  • Haemodialysis machine is commonly called an artificial kidney in textbooks.
  • It removes urea and other diffusible wastes from blood.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Artificial Kidney → Dialysis Machine

121. Nervous System

The nervous system coordinates rapid body responses.

It is divided into:

  • Central nervous system.
  • Peripheral nervous system.
122. Central Nervous System

CNS consists of:

  • Brain.
  • Spinal cord.
📌 Must-Memorise

CNS → Brain + Spinal Cord

123. Peripheral Nervous System
  • PNS consists of nerves outside brain and spinal cord.
  • It links the CNS with receptors, muscles and glands.
124. Neuron
  • Neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.
  • Main parts are dendrites, cell body and axon.
  • Dendrites generally receive signals.
  • Axons generally conduct impulses away from cell body.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nervous System Unit → Neuron

125. Myelin
  • Myelin is an insulating covering around many axons.
  • It increases speed of nerve-impulse conduction.
  • Schwann cells form myelin in the peripheral nervous system.
  • Oligodendrocytes form myelin in the CNS.
126. Synapse
  • Synapse is the junction between two neurons or between a neuron and another cell.
  • Chemical synapses use neurotransmitters.
  • Neurotransmitters cross a narrow synaptic cleft.
127. Neurotransmitters

Examples include:

  • Acetylcholine.
  • Dopamine.
  • Serotonin.
  • GABA.
  • Glutamate.
  • Noradrenaline.
128. Brain

Major divisions include:

  • Forebrain.
  • Midbrain.
  • Hindbrain.

Important structures include:

  • Cerebrum.
  • Thalamus.
  • Hypothalamus.
  • Cerebellum.
  • Pons.
  • Medulla oblongata.
129. Cerebrum
  • Cerebrum is the largest part of the human brain.
  • It is involved in conscious thought, memory, sensation and voluntary movement.
  • It is divided into right and left cerebral hemispheres.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Largest Brain Part → Cerebrum

130. Cerebral Lobes

Major lobes are:

  • Frontal.
  • Parietal.
  • Temporal.
  • Occipital.
131. Frontal Lobe
  • Frontal lobe is involved in voluntary motor control.
  • It contributes to planning, decision-making and personality.
  • Broca's area is usually located in the dominant frontal lobe and is important for speech production.
132. Parietal Lobe
  • Parietal lobe processes touch and other somatic sensations.
  • It contributes to spatial awareness.
133. Temporal Lobe
  • Temporal lobe participates in hearing.
  • It is important in memory and language comprehension.
  • Wernicke's area is usually located in the dominant temporal region.
134. Occipital Lobe
  • Occipital lobe is the major visual-processing region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Occipital Lobe → Vision

135. Cerebellum
  • Cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and fine voluntary movements.
  • It does not initiate conscious movement.
  • It fine-tunes motor activity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cerebellum → Balance + Coordination

136. Medulla Oblongata
  • Medulla controls vital involuntary functions.
  • These include breathing, heart rate and blood-vessel regulation.
  • It also coordinates reflexes such as swallowing and coughing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Medulla → Vital Involuntary Functions

137. Hypothalamus
  • Hypothalamus links nervous and endocrine systems.
  • It regulates body temperature.
  • It influences hunger and thirst.
  • It controls pituitary hormone secretion.
  • It synthesises ADH and oxytocin.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hypothalamus → Homeostatic Control

138. Spinal Cord
  • Spinal cord conducts signals between brain and body.
  • It also acts as a centre for many reflex actions.
  • It is protected within the vertebral column.
139. Reflex Action
  • Reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus.
  • Many reflexes occur without conscious processing before the response.
  • Withdrawal from a painful stimulus is a classic example.
140. Reflex Arc

Typical reflex arc:

Receptor → Sensory neuron → CNS/interneuron → Motor neuron → Effector

📌 Must-Memorise

Reflex Arc → Receptor → Sensory → CNS → Motor → Effector

141. Autonomic Nervous System
  • Autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary functions.
  • It controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands.
  • Major divisions are sympathetic and parasympathetic.
142. Sympathetic Division
  • Sympathetic system prepares body for activity or stress.
  • Heart rate increases.
  • Pupils dilate.
  • Blood flow is redirected toward skeletal muscles.
  • Digestive activity generally decreases.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sympathetic → Fight or Flight

143. Parasympathetic Division
  • Parasympathetic system supports rest and recovery.
  • Heart rate generally decreases.
  • Digestive activity increases.
  • Energy is conserved.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Parasympathetic → Rest and Digest

144. Endocrine System
  • Endocrine glands release hormones directly into blood.
  • Hormones act as chemical messengers.
  • They act on target cells possessing suitable receptors.
  • Hormonal responses are generally slower but longer-lasting than nerve impulses.
145. Endocrine vs Exocrine Glands
  • Endocrine glands are ductless.
  • Exocrine glands release secretions through ducts.
  • Pituitary is endocrine.
  • Salivary glands are exocrine.
  • Pancreas has both endocrine and exocrine functions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Endocrine → Ductless.

146. Major Endocrine Glands

Important glands include:

  • Pituitary.
  • Thyroid.
  • Parathyroids.
  • Adrenals.
  • Pancreatic islets.
  • Pineal.
  • Thymus.
  • Ovaries.
  • Testes.
147. Pituitary Gland
  • Pituitary lies below the hypothalamus.
  • It is often called the master gland in traditional textbooks.
  • Many pituitary hormones regulate other endocrine glands.
  • Its activity itself is largely controlled by hypothalamus.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pituitary → Master Gland in Traditional Textbooks

148. Growth Hormone
  • Growth hormone is secreted by anterior pituitary.
  • It promotes growth of bones and other tissues.
  • It also influences metabolism.
149. TSH
  • TSH stands for thyroid-stimulating hormone.
  • It is produced by anterior pituitary.
  • It stimulates thyroid hormone production.
150. ACTH
  • ACTH stands for adrenocorticotropic hormone.
  • It is secreted by anterior pituitary.
  • It stimulates adrenal cortex, especially cortisol secretion.
151. FSH and LH
  • FSH stands for follicle-stimulating hormone.
  • LH stands for luteinising hormone.
  • They regulate reproductive organs.
  • In females, they regulate follicle development and ovulation.
  • In males, they regulate sperm production and testosterone-related functions.
152. Posterior Pituitary Hormones

Posterior pituitary releases:

  • ADH.
  • Oxytocin.
  • These hormones are synthesised in hypothalamus.
153. Oxytocin
  • Oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions during childbirth.
  • It causes milk ejection from mammary glands.
  • It is released from posterior pituitary.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Oxytocin → Milk ejection.

Prolactin → Milk production.

154. Prolactin
  • Prolactin is secreted by anterior pituitary.
  • It stimulates milk production after childbirth.
155. Thyroid Gland
  • Thyroid gland lies in the neck.
  • It produces thyroxine/T4 and triiodothyronine/T3.
  • These hormones regulate metabolic rate, growth and development.
  • Iodine is required for thyroid hormone synthesis.
📌 Must-Memorise

Thyroid Hormone → Requires Iodine

156. Calcitonin
  • Calcitonin is produced by thyroid C cells.
  • It helps lower blood calcium levels in appropriate physiological conditions.
  • Its role in adult calcium homeostasis is less dominant than parathyroid hormone.
157. Parathyroid Glands
  • Parathyroid glands are usually four small glands on the posterior thyroid.
  • They secrete parathyroid hormone.
  • PTH raises blood calcium concentration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PTH → Blood Calcium ↑

158. Pancreatic Islets
  • Islets of Langerhans form the endocrine part of pancreas.
  • Beta cells secrete insulin.
  • Alpha cells secrete glucagon.
  • Delta cells secrete somatostatin.
📌 Must-Memorise

Beta → Insulin

Alpha → Glucagon

159. Insulin
  • Insulin lowers blood glucose.
  • It increases cellular glucose uptake in insulin-sensitive tissues.
  • It promotes glycogen formation.
  • It promotes storage of nutrients.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Insulin → Blood Glucose ↓

160. Glucagon
  • Glucagon raises blood glucose.
  • It promotes breakdown of liver glycogen.
  • It promotes glucose production by the liver.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Glucagon → Blood Glucose ↑

161. Adrenal Glands
  • Adrenal glands lie above kidneys.
  • Each gland has an outer cortex and inner medulla.
  • Cortex and medulla produce different hormones.
162. Adrenal Medulla
  • Adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline.
  • These hormones support fight-or-flight responses.
  • They increase heart rate and mobilise energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Adrenaline → Fight or Flight

163. Adrenal Cortex

Major hormones include:

  • Cortisol.
  • Aldosterone.
  • Adrenal androgens.
164. Cortisol
  • Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone.
  • It helps regulate metabolism.
  • It participates in stress responses.
  • Excess or deficiency alters normal physiology.
165. Aldosterone
  • Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid.
  • It promotes sodium retention.
  • It promotes potassium excretion.
  • It contributes to blood-volume regulation.
166. Pineal Gland
  • Pineal gland produces melatonin.
  • Melatonin helps regulate circadian rhythms and sleep-wake timing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pineal → Melatonin → Biological Clock

167. Thymus
  • Thymus is important in development and maturation of T lymphocytes.
  • It is relatively large in children.
  • It undergoes involution after puberty.
  • Thymic hormones participate in immune development.
168. Testes
  • Testes produce sperm.
  • Leydig cells produce testosterone.
  • Sertoli cells support developing sperm cells.
  • Testes function as both reproductive organs and endocrine glands.
169. Ovaries
  • Ovaries produce ova.
  • They produce estrogen and progesterone.
  • These hormones regulate reproductive cycles and secondary sexual characteristics.
170. Negative Feedback
  • Most endocrine systems are regulated by negative feedback.
  • When hormone effect or concentration rises, further secretion is reduced.
  • Thyroid hormone regulation is a classic example.
171. Skeletal System
  • Adult human skeleton contains approximately 206 bones.
  • The skeleton supports the body.
  • It protects internal organs.
  • It provides attachment sites for muscles.
  • Bone marrow forms blood cells.
📌 Must-Memorise

Adult Human Bones → 206

172. Axial Skeleton

Axial skeleton includes:

  • Skull.
  • Vertebral column.
  • Ribs.
  • Sternum.
  • It forms the central body axis.
173. Appendicular Skeleton

Appendicular skeleton includes:

  • Shoulder girdles.
  • Upper limbs.
  • Pelvic girdle.
  • Lower limbs.
174. Longest Bone
  • Femur is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.
  • It is located in the thigh.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Longest Bone → Femur

175. Smallest Bone
  • Stapes is the smallest bone in the human body.
  • It is located in the middle ear.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Smallest Bone → Stapes

176. Vertebral Column
  • Human vertebral column develops from 33 vertebral elements.
  • In adults, fusion produces approximately 26 separate bones.
  • Regions are cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal.
📌 Traditional Count

Cervical → 7.

Thoracic → 12.

Lumbar → 5.

Sacral → 5 fused.

Coccygeal → Usually 4 fused.

177. Ribs
  • Humans normally possess 12 pairs of ribs.
  • First seven pairs are commonly called true ribs.
  • Pairs 8–10 are false ribs attached indirectly.
  • Pairs 11 and 12 are floating ribs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Human Ribs → 12 Pairs

178. Joints

Major joint types include:

  • Fibrous.
  • Cartilaginous.
  • Synovial.
  • Synovial joints allow the greatest movement.
179. Ball-and-Socket Joint

Examples:

  • Shoulder.
  • Hip.
  • It allows movement in several directions.
180. Hinge Joint

Examples:

  • Elbow.
  • Knee in simplified textbook classification.
  • It mainly allows flexion and extension.
181. Pivot Joint
  • Pivot joint permits rotational movement.
  • Joint between atlas and axis contributes to head rotation.
182. Skeletal Muscle
  • Skeletal muscle is striated.
  • It is mainly under voluntary control.
  • It attaches to bones through tendons.
  • Muscle contraction produces body movement.
183. Smooth Muscle
  • Smooth muscle is non-striated.
  • It is involuntary.
  • It occurs in walls of intestine, blood vessels and many internal organs.
184. Cardiac Muscle
  • Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.
  • It is striated but involuntary.
  • Cells are connected by intercalated discs.
  • Cardiac muscle has intrinsic rhythmic activity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cardiac → Striated + Involuntary

185. Tendon
  • Tendon connects muscle to bone.
  • Tendons contain strong collagen fibres.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tendon → Muscle to Bone

186. Ligament
  • Ligament connects bone to bone.
  • Ligaments stabilise joints.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ligament → Bone to Bone

187. Muscle Contraction
  • Skeletal muscle contraction involves actin and myosin.
  • The sliding-filament mechanism shortens sarcomeres.
  • ATP is required.
  • Calcium ions are essential for normal contraction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Muscle Contraction → Actin + Myosin + ATP + Ca²⁺

188. Sarcomere
  • Sarcomere is the basic contractile unit of striated muscle.
  • It extends between two Z lines.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Muscle Contractile Unit → Sarcomere

189. Sense Organs

Major sense organs include:

  • Eye → Vision.
  • Ear → Hearing and balance.
  • Nose → Smell.
  • Tongue → Taste.
  • Skin → Touch, temperature and pain.
190. Human Eye

Important parts include:

  • Cornea.
  • Iris.
  • Pupil.
  • Lens.
  • Retina.
  • Optic nerve.
191. Cornea
  • Cornea is the transparent front surface of the eye.
  • It provides much of the eye's refractive power.
  • It has no blood vessels under normal conditions.
192. Iris
  • Iris is the coloured part of the eye.
  • It contains muscles controlling pupil diameter.
193. Pupil
  • Pupil is the opening through which light enters the eye.
  • It becomes smaller in bright light.
  • It enlarges in dim light.
194. Lens
  • Lens focuses light on the retina.
  • Ciliary muscles alter lens shape.
  • This process is called accommodation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Accommodation → Change in Lens Curvature

195. Retina
  • Retina contains photoreceptors.
  • Rods detect low-intensity light.
  • Cones are responsible for colour vision and high visual acuity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rods → Dim Light

Cones → Colour

196. Yellow Spot
  • Fovea centralis is the region of highest visual acuity.
  • It contains a very high density of cones.
  • It lies within the macular region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sharpest Vision → Fovea

197. Blind Spot
  • Blind spot is where optic nerve leaves the retina.
  • Photoreceptors are absent at this point.
  • Therefore, light falling exactly on the blind spot is not detected.
198. Ear

The ear has:

  • Outer ear.
  • Middle ear.
  • Inner ear.
199. Middle-Ear Ossicles

Three small bones are:

  • Malleus.
  • Incus.
  • Stapes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Malleus → Incus → Stapes

200. Cochlea
  • Cochlea is involved in hearing.
  • It contains the organ of Corti.
  • Hair cells convert mechanical vibrations into nerve signals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cochlea → Hearing

201. Semicircular Canals
  • Semicircular canals detect rotational head movements.
  • They help maintain dynamic equilibrium.
  • The vestibular apparatus also includes utricle and saccule.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Semicircular Canals → Balance

202. Taste Receptors
  • Taste buds contain sensory receptor cells.
  • Major recognised taste qualities are sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.
  • Different regions of the tongue are not exclusively restricted to one taste.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

The old rigid “tongue taste map” is inaccurate.

203. Smell
  • Olfactory receptors are present in the upper nasal cavity.
  • Odorant molecules stimulate these receptors.
  • Smell and taste interact strongly in flavour perception.
204. Skin
  • Skin is the largest organ of the human body.
  • It protects against physical and microbial damage.
  • It reduces water loss.
  • It contains sensory receptors.
  • It contributes to temperature regulation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Largest Human Organ → Skin

205. Skin Layers

Major layers are:

  • Epidermis.
  • Dermis.
  • Subcutaneous tissue lies below the skin.
206. Sweat Glands
  • Sweat glands produce sweat.
  • Evaporation of sweat cools the body.
  • Sweat contains water and salts.
207. Body Temperature
  • Normal core body temperature is approximately 37°C.
  • It varies slightly during the day and among individuals.
  • Hypothalamus is the major thermoregulatory centre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Temperature Regulation → Hypothalamus

208. Cooling Mechanisms

When body temperature rises:

  • Skin blood vessels dilate.
  • Sweating increases.
  • Heat loss increases.
209. Heat Conservation

When body temperature falls:

  • Skin blood vessels constrict.
  • Sweating decreases.
  • Shivering may generate heat.
  • Metabolic heat production can increase.
210. Male Reproductive System

Important structures include:

  • Testes.
  • Epididymis.
  • Vas deferens.
  • Seminal vesicles.
  • Prostate.
  • Penis.
211. Testes
  • Testes are located in the scrotum.
  • Sperm production occurs in seminiferous tubules.
  • Testosterone is produced mainly by Leydig cells.
  • Testicular temperature is normally slightly below core body temperature.
212. Spermatogenesis
  • Spermatogenesis is formation of sperm cells.
  • It begins at puberty.
  • It occurs in seminiferous tubules.
  • Meiosis reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Human Sperm → Haploid → 23 Chromosomes

213. Epididymis
  • Sperm mature and are stored temporarily in the epididymis.
  • Epididymis lies along the posterior side of each testis.
214. Vas Deferens
  • Vas deferens transports sperm from epididymis toward the ejaculatory ducts.
215. Seminal Vesicles
  • Seminal vesicles contribute a major portion of seminal fluid.
  • Their secretion contains fructose and other substances supporting sperm.
216. Prostate Gland
  • Prostate contributes fluid to semen.
  • Its secretions support sperm function.
217. Female Reproductive System

Important structures include:

  • Ovaries.
  • Fallopian tubes/oviducts.
  • Uterus.
  • Cervix.
  • Vagina.
218. Oogenesis
  • Oogenesis is formation of female gametes.
  • It begins before birth.
  • Primary oocytes remain arrested for long periods.
  • Usually one secondary oocyte is released during each ovulatory cycle.
219. Ovulation
  • Ovulation is release of a secondary oocyte from the ovary.
  • In a typical 28-day cycle, it occurs around day 14.
  • Actual timing varies among individuals and cycles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Typical 28-Day Cycle → Ovulation Around Day 14

220. Menstrual Cycle

Major phases include:

  • Menstrual phase.
  • Follicular/proliferative phase.
  • Ovulation.
  • Luteal/secretory phase.
  • A typical cycle averages around 28 days but normal cycles vary considerably.
221. FSH
  • FSH promotes ovarian follicle development.
  • It stimulates estrogen production by developing follicles.
222. LH Surge
  • A surge in luteinising hormone triggers ovulation.
  • LH also promotes formation of the corpus luteum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ovulation Trigger → LH Surge

223. Corpus Luteum
  • Corpus luteum develops from the ruptured follicle after ovulation.
  • It secretes progesterone and some estrogen.
  • Progesterone supports the uterine lining.
224. Fertilisation
  • Fertilisation is fusion of sperm and ovum.
  • In humans it usually occurs in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube.
  • Fertilisation restores diploid chromosome number.
📌 Must-Memorise

Usual Human Fertilisation Site → Fallopian Tube/Ampulla

225. Zygote
  • Zygote is the first diploid cell formed after fertilisation.
  • It undergoes repeated mitotic divisions called cleavage.
226. Implantation
  • The developing blastocyst reaches the uterus.
  • Implantation occurs in the endometrium.
  • It normally begins about a week after fertilisation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Implantation → Uterine Endometrium

227. Placenta
  • Placenta is a temporary organ connecting mother and developing fetus.
  • It permits exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes.
  • Maternal and fetal blood normally do not directly mix extensively.
  • Placenta also secretes hormones.
228. hCG
  • hCG stands for human chorionic gonadotropin.
  • It is produced after implantation mainly by placental trophoblast tissue.
  • It maintains corpus luteum in early pregnancy.
  • Pregnancy tests detect hCG.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pregnancy Test → hCG

229. Human Gestation
  • Human pregnancy lasts approximately 38 weeks from fertilisation.
  • Clinically it is approximately 40 weeks or 280 days from the last menstrual period.
📌 Must-Memorise

Human Gestation → ~280 Days

230. Parturition
  • Parturition means childbirth.
  • Oxytocin contributes to uterine contractions.
  • Positive-feedback mechanisms intensify contractions during labour.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Parturition → Oxytocin

231. Lactation
  • Lactation is milk production after childbirth.
  • Prolactin promotes milk synthesis.
  • Oxytocin causes milk ejection.
📌 Must-Memorise

Prolactin → Milk Production

Oxytocin → Milk Ejection

232. Colostrum
  • Colostrum is the first milk produced after childbirth.
  • It is rich in antibodies, especially secretory IgA.
  • It provides important early immune protection to the newborn.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Colostrum → Antibody-Rich First Milk

233. Feedback Regulation of Blood Glucose

After blood glucose rises:

  • Insulin secretion increases.
  • Cells take up/store glucose.
  • Blood glucose decreases.

When blood glucose falls:

  • Glucagon secretion increases.
  • Liver releases glucose.
  • Blood glucose rises.
234. Water Balance
  • Hypothalamus detects changes in body-fluid concentration.
  • ADH secretion increases during dehydration.
  • Kidneys reabsorb more water.
  • Urine becomes more concentrated.
235. Acid-Base Balance

Major regulators are:

  • Chemical buffers.
  • Lungs.
  • Kidneys.
  • Lungs regulate carbon dioxide.
  • Kidneys regulate hydrogen ions and bicarbonate.
236. Plant Physiology — Water Absorption
  • Plant roots absorb water mainly through root hairs.
  • Water enters root cells primarily by osmosis.
  • Mineral ions can be absorbed by active transport.
  • Water eventually enters xylem.
237. Xylem Transport
  • Xylem carries water and mineral ions from roots toward shoots.
  • Transpiration pull is a major driving force.
  • Cohesion between water molecules helps maintain a continuous column.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Xylem → Water + Minerals

238. Transpiration
  • Transpiration is loss of water vapour from aerial plant surfaces.
  • Most water is lost through stomata.
  • Transpiration helps cool leaves.
  • It contributes to upward movement of water.
239. Stomata
  • Stomata are microscopic pores in leaf epidermis.
  • Guard cells regulate stomatal opening.
  • Carbon dioxide enters through stomata.
  • Oxygen and water vapour can leave through stomata.
240. Phloem Translocation
  • Phloem transports sugars and other organic solutes.
  • Sugar usually moves from a source to a sink.
  • Leaves are common sources.
  • Roots, fruits and growing tissues can act as sinks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phloem → Food Translocation

241. Photosynthesis
  • Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy.
  • Chloroplasts are the main photosynthetic organelles.
  • Chlorophyll absorbs light.
  • Carbon dioxide and water are used.
  • Oxygen is released.
📌 Simplified Equation

6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

242. Light Reactions
  • Light-dependent reactions occur in thylakoid membranes.
  • They generate ATP and NADPH.
  • Water is split.
  • Oxygen is released.
243. Calvin Cycle
  • Carbon fixation occurs through the Calvin cycle.
  • It occurs in chloroplast stroma.
  • The enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

RuBisCO → CO₂ Fixation

244. Plant Respiration
  • Plants respire continuously.
  • Cellular respiration occurs day and night.
  • Photosynthesis requires suitable light.
  • Plant respiration releases usable energy as ATP.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Plants do not stop respiration during daytime.

245. Phototropism
  • Shoots commonly grow toward light.
  • This is positive phototropism.
  • Auxin redistribution contributes to differential growth.
246. Gravitropism
  • Roots normally show positive gravitropism.
  • Shoots normally show negative gravitropism.
247. Plant Hormones — Quick Link
  • Auxin → Cell elongation/apical dominance.
  • Gibberellin → Stem elongation/germination.
  • Cytokinin → Cell division.
  • ABA → Dormancy/stomatal closure.
  • Ethylene → Fruit ripening.
248. Photoperiodism
  • Photoperiodism is a plant's physiological response to relative lengths of day and night.
  • It influences flowering in many plants.
  • Phytochrome participates in light sensing.
249. Vernalisation
  • Vernalisation is promotion of flowering by exposure to prolonged cold.
  • It occurs in some winter cereals and biennial plants.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vernalisation → Cold-Induced Flowering Response
